proposed one such technique called the 'surface code.' The surface code is a very surprisingly simple scheme. We just place our qubits
on a square lattice and then perform local measurements on these qubits. With the surface code, qubits are arranged in overlapping grids consisting of data qubits and error-measurement qubits.

information in a very carefully orchestrated way,
such that we can check for local errors. And this collection of physical qubits
functions as a single, high quality logical qubit. We have many qubits work together
to express a single, more perfect qubit, and that single logical qubit is more

the error-correction.

code, the team finally put their new 72-qubit processor,

error-suppression improvement just on this first run. Seeing it work

the whole system is working well together, where we can actually see the exponential

as we increase the code size.

a demonstration that things work. We know now that we can build devices

is managing trade-offs between computational speed
or time, and space and memory. We want to minimize the time

and space was essentially fixed. If a computation
used a certain amount of time, it will probably use roughly
that amount of space. Now, in a groundbreaking paper,

that converts any algorithm to save a substantial amount of space.
